deck: First aid in the field
front: Order of care for an injured hunter?
back: Scene safe (guns unloaded), call for help, stop big bleeding, breathing, keep warm.

deck: First aid in the field
front: What are the 3 steps of the first minute?
back: Check (scene and danger), Call (911 or SOS, location first), Care (bleeding first).

deck: First aid in the field
front: On a 911 call, what do you say first?
back: Your location. If the call drops, help still knows where to go.

deck: First aid in the field
front: No bars from your carrier. Can 911 still work?
back: Often yes: a phone can reach 911 through any carrier tower in range (BC Search and Rescue Association, 75%).

deck: First aid in the field
front: Name 4 signs of life threatening bleeding.
back: Spurting, flowing that will not slow, pooling on the ground, soaking through clothes. Also a missing limb or a confused, pale person.

deck: First aid in the field
front: The bleeding control ladder?
back: Press, pack, tourniquet. Climb only as far as you need.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Which wounds get packed instead of a tourniquet?
back: Deep wounds in the groin, armpit or side of the neck. Not the chest or belly.

deck: First aid in the field
front: After packing a wound, how long do you press on top?
back: At least 3 minutes, then wrap tight. Do not peek.

deck: First aid in the field
front: When does a tourniquet go on?
back: Life threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that direct pressure cannot control.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Where does a tourniquet go?
back: Above the wound on the heart side, never on a joint. Distance: 5 to 8 cm or 5 to 10 cm depending on source (VERIFY with your instructor).

deck: First aid in the field
front: How do you finish a tourniquet?
back: Twist till it stops, lock, clock: lock the rod in its clip, write the time, leave it on for the medics.

deck: First aid in the field
front: First tourniquet as tight as it goes, still bleeding?
back: Add a second tourniquet above the first, closer to the heart.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Signs of shock and the care?
back: Pale, cold, clammy, fast pulse, thirst, confusion. Stop bleeding, lay flat on a pad, cover, nothing to eat or drink.

deck: First aid in the field
front: How do you clean a dirty knife cut in the bush?
back: Flush with at least 1 litre of drinkable water under pressure (squeezed bottle or pin hole bag), then cover.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Signs a cut is infected?
back: Spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, a red streak, fever. See a doctor.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Two habits that prevent gutting cuts?
back: Cut away from you with fingers behind the blade, and wipe the handle so a bloody grip does not slide.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Rolled ankle: field care?
back: Sit, look for a bad bend, cool in a cloth 10 to 20 minutes, wrap firm, foot up, then the 4 step test.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Hurt leg: what decides walk out or wait?
back: Can take 4 steps: wrap, poles, partner carries gear. Cannot: stay, splint, shelter, call for help.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Splint rules?
back: Do not straighten. Pad. Joint above to joint below. Ties off the break. Check warmth and feeling before and after.

deck: First aid in the field
front: Trauma kit contents?
back: Tourniquet, pressure bandage, packing gauze, gloves, shears, marker and tape. On your body, same pocket every hunt.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Name the 4 ways your body loses heat.
back: Conduction (cold ground), convection (wind), radiation (open sky), evaporation (sweat, wet clothes).

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: What is the hunter cold trap?
back: Sweating on the climb, then sitting still to glass in damp clothes as the day cools.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Kamloops Airport October average low and November average low?
back: October 3.5 °C, November minus 1.1 °C (1991 to 2020). Higher ground is colder.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: About when is sunset in Kamloops on 31 October?
back: About 17:40, dark by about 18:14 (calculated). Clocks fall back 1 November.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: The 4 stay dry habits?
back: Start a little cold, vent before you sweat, swap a soaked base layer, puffy on and pad under when you stop.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Signs of mild hypothermia?
back: Alert but shivering strongly, clumsy movement. Core about 35 to 32 °C.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Signs of moderate hypothermia?
back: Shivering slows or stops, drowsy but conscious. Core about 32 to 28 °C.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Signs of severe hypothermia?
back: No shivering, not conscious. Core under 28 °C. Check breathing and pulse up to 60 seconds.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: What are the umbles?
back: Stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles: early hypothermia signs.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Field care for mild hypothermia?
back: Out of wind and wet, pad under, dry layers, head covered, heat to armpits, chest and back, warm sweet food if alert, rest 30 minutes.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Care for moderate or severe hypothermia?
back: Gentle, flat, no food or drink, insulate, big heat on the upper trunk, tarp outside, call 911 or SOS.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Are small hand warmers enough to rewarm a cold core?
back: No. Use large heat sources on the trunk. Small packs only for hands and feet.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: What is afterdrop?
back: Cold blood from the limbs returning to the core when limbs are warmed or moved, dropping core temperature. Warm the trunk first, move gently.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Frostnip or frostbite: how to tell?
back: Frostnip is surface only and comes back fast with warming. Frostbite freezes tissue: white, waxy, hard.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Should you rub frostbite or rub snow on it?
back: No. Never rub. Blot dry.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: When should you NOT thaw frostbite?
back: When it could refreeze before you reach care. Thaw then refreeze does the most damage.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Frostbite rewarming water temperature and time?
back: 37 to 39 °C, about 30 minutes, until soft and red or purple.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Minus 23 °C with a 48 km/h wind: how fast can skin freeze?
back: About 10 minutes (US National Weather Service chart).

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Mitts or gloves for warmth?
back: Mitts. Carry gloves for fine work.

deck: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather
front: Why carry a foam sit pad?
back: It stops conduction: cold ground or a log pulls heat out of you for hours.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: What does STOP stand for?
back: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan (AdventureSmart).

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Name 3 ways hunters get lost.
back: Chasing wounded game, darkness falling, fog or snow, head down on a track, a shortcut back, never looking back.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Why stay put when lost?
back: It reduces the time and the area searchers must cover.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: You wander twice as far. How much bigger is the search area?
back: 4 times. Area grows with the distance squared.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Can you walk straight in thick timber under cloud?
back: Usually not. Studies show people curve and even cross their own path without sun or landmarks.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Lost in steep country: follow the creek downhill?
back: Not by default. Creeks drop into ravines and canyons that are hard to climb out of.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: First action when you need rescue?
back: Call 911. Police dispatch Search and Rescue.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Your carrier has no signal. Can 911 still connect?
back: Often yes, through any carrier tower in range.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: On the call, what do you say first?
back: Your location or coordinates.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: No signal at all. What next?
back: Satellite SOS (iPhone 14 or later in Canada, or a satellite messenger) from open sky.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Where does the phone ride in the cold, and why?
back: Inside pocket against your body. Cold drains batteries and can shut the phone off (iPhone range 0 to 35 °C).

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Distress signal pattern?
back: Anything in threes: 3 whistle blasts, 3 flashes, 3 fires, 3 rock piles.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Ground to air signal and size?
back: A V or SOS at least 3 m long, high contrast.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Three ways to help searchers find you?
back: Settle at the edge of an opening, spread orange and bright gear, whistle 3 times when you hear them.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Why a whistle instead of shouting?
back: It carries farther and costs no energy.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Best habit to avoid getting lost?
back: Pin the truck, look back at every junction, carry map and compass, set a turn back time.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Pocket survival kit contents?
back: 2 lighters, fire starter, whistle, space blanket or bivy, headlamp, knife, water bag, cord.

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: The 3 layers of kit?
back: Pockets (go everywhere), day pack (10 essentials, shelter), truck (food, sleeping bag, extras).

deck: Lost: what to do, and the survival kit
front: Lost overnight: priorities in order?
back: Calm and STOP, call or signal, shelter and warmth, fire, water, food last.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: What 3 things does fire need?
back: Heat, fuel and air. Wet fuel steals heat; packed wood starves air.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Size limit of a Category 1 campfire?
back: One pile no larger than 0.5 m high and 0.5 m wide.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: What must stand by while a campfire burns?
back: At least 8 litres of water or a hand tool (check the current order wording).

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Before every fire, check what?
back: The BC Wildfire Service ban status for your fire centre.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Fine for breaking an open fire ban?
back: Up to $1,150. An escaped fire causing a wildfire: up to $1 million, jail and firefighting costs.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Where is dry fuel in the rain?
back: Standing dead wood, dead twigs under big spruce, the split core of a log, birch bark, pitch wood, your pocket fire starter.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: How do you test if a stick is dry?
back: Dry dead wood snaps. Wet or green wood bends.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: What is pitch wood?
back: Resin soaked wood from old pine or fir stumps and knots. Burns even when the outside is wet.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: The fuel ladder sizes?
back: Tinder, matchstick, pencil, thumb, wrist. 2 big handfuls of each before you light.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: What is a feather stick?
back: A split dry stick shaved into thin curls left attached. Catches from a lighter in rain.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Why build a platform first?
back: It keeps tinder off wet ground or snow.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Where is the door of the tipi?
back: On the upwind side, so wind feeds air into the tinder.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Where do you light the tinder?
back: Low, at the bottom, from the upwind side, shielded by your body.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: How many ways to light should you carry?
back: Two, in two pockets: lighter plus fire starter, and matches or a ferro rod.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Tarp over a fire?
back: High above it, never close. Tarps melt and burn.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: How do you make signal smoke by day?
back: Green boughs on a hot fire, in the open. Three fires mean help.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Putting a fire out in 4 words?
back: Drown, stir, feel, repeat. Cool to the touch everywhere.

deck: Fire: building one in wet BC weather
front: Report a wildfire: number?
back: 1 800 663 5555 toll free, or *5555 on a cell.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Shelter priority: bed or roof?
back: Bed first, roof second. The ground pulls heat by conduction all night.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: When do you start building?
back: At least an hour before dark, when the light turns gold and you are still far from the truck.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Best spot for a night out?
back: A sheltered bench part way up, near trees, fuel and an opening. Not the valley bottom, not the windy top.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Why not sleep in the valley bottom?
back: Cold air sinks and pools there at night, and it is often wet.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Before you settle, look where?
back: Up: no dead trees or hanging branches over you.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: What makes a good bed?
back: Foam pad, pack, boughs, dry grass or leaves, thick enough to stay a hand thick when you lie on it.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Tarp shelter in 4 steps?
back: Tight cord between trees, drape the tarp, pin the windward edge low, bed underneath.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Which side of the tarp faces the wind?
back: The low pinned edge. The open side faces away.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: What is a foil blanket bad at?
back: Stopping heat loss into the ground. It also tears and traps moisture.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Foil blanket or bivy bag?
back: Bivy bag in the pack (wraps you, stops wind); foil blanket as pocket backup. Both need a bed under.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Debris hut steps?
back: Pole from a stump to the ground, close ribs, pile debris thick, fill the inside, plug the door.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Downside of a debris hut?
back: It takes hours and lots of dry material. A tarp is faster.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: How does a reflector wall help?
back: Logs or rocks behind a small fire bounce heat back toward you.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Fire or stove inside a closed shelter?
back: Never. Carbon monoxide and fire risk.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Night routine?
back: Eat, pee, dry socks on, toque on all night, boots in a bag. Cold: eat and move.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Two hunters, one night out?
back: One bed, one cover, back to back. Colder or hurt person in the middle of the insulation.

deck: Shelter: surviving an unplanned night out
front: Shelter hidden in thick timber. Problem?
back: Searchers cannot see you. Put orange and bright gear in the nearest opening.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: A creek looks crystal clear. Safe to drink?
back: No. Treat every lake, creek and spring. Germs are invisible.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: What is beaver fever?
back: Giardiasis, a gut infection from the Giardia parasite, mostly from contaminated water.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: When do Giardia symptoms usually start, and how long do they last?
back: Usually 1 to 3 weeks after infection; they can last 2 to 6 weeks.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Boiling time for safe water?
back: Rolling boil at least 1 minute; above 2,000 m at least 2 minutes (HealthLink BC).

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Filter pore size for Giardia?
back: 1 micron or smaller, certified (NSF). Jug filters like Brita do not count.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Does a backcountry filter stop viruses?
back: No. Boiling, chemicals or UV do.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Bleach dose for 1 litre of clear water?
back: 2 drops of unscented household bleach, wait 30 minutes.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Bleach in cloudy or cold (under 10 °C) water?
back: Double the dose and wait 1 to 2 hours.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Is chlorine good against Giardia?
back: Generally not effective. Boil or filter for Giardia.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Cloudy water: what first?
back: Strain through cloth, let it settle, pour off the clear water, then treat.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Weak spot of a UV pen?
back: Only works in small amounts of clear water. Particles shield germs.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Green scum or a fuel sheen: boil it?
back: No. Boiling does not remove toxins or chemicals. Find other water.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Signs of water in dry Interior hills?
back: A green line of brush in a draw, cottonwood and willow, seeps below rock outcrops.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Best to worst water sources?
back: Spring at its source, fast clear creek, lake away from shore, pond or slough or cattle water last.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Toilet distance from water?
back: At least 30 m.

deck: Water: finding it and making it safe
front: Why keep the filter warm in November?
back: Many hollow fibre filters can be damaged by freezing. Check the maker.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Rule one with bears and cougars?
back: Never run. Stop, stay calm.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Why do hunters meet more bears?
back: Quiet movement, dawn and dusk, blood and gut piles, calls and decoys, thick cover, kill sites.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Where should you call out to avoid surprising a bear?
back: Near running water, thick brush, berry patches and in high wind.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: You find a carcass you did not shoot. What do you do?
back: Leave the area at once and report it. A bear may be guarding it.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Bear has not noticed you?
back: Leave quietly the way you came, watching it, spray ready.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Bear sees you but is calm?
back: Speak softly and back away slowly. Do not follow it.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Signs of an agitated bear?
back: Jaw popping, woofing, moaning, stomping, bluff charging.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Bear keeps coming steadily toward you?
back: May be predatory. Yell, stand big, move to high ground, spray, be ready to fight.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: At what distance does WildSafeBC say to spray?
back: When the bear is within about 5 to 10 m.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Where do you carry bear spray?
back: Chest or hip holster. Never in the pack.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Spray or gun: which stopped bears more often in studies?
back: Spray: about 92% versus about 67% for guns (as reported for the Smith and Herrero studies).

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Defensive bear makes contact. What do you do?
back: Lie on your stomach, pack on, hands over the back of your neck, legs apart. Stay still until it leaves.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Predatory bear attack?
back: Fight back with everything, at the face, eyes and nose.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: How far from the gut pile should the meat go?
back: At least 200 m (Alberta guidance). Bears often go to the gut pile first.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: How high and how far from trunks do you hang meat?
back: At least 3.5 m up and 1.5 m from tree trunks, in view from a distance.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Going back to your meat: how?
back: From upwind, stop and glass it, call out. Bear on it, or moved or buried: leave and report.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Drag the carcass back to camp?
back: No. It lays a scent trail to where you sleep.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Camp distances in bear country?
back: Food, cooking and meat at least 100 m from where you sleep. Never food in the tent.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Cougar encounter steps?
back: Never run, look big, eye contact, loud voice, back away slowly, leave it an exit. Attacked: fight, face and eyes.

deck: Bears and cougars: avoiding and handling encounters
front: Number to report an aggressive bear or cougar?
back: 1 877 952 7277 (RAPP and Conservation Officer Service line).

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: The 4 checks before a fire season hunt?
back: Fire map, area restriction orders, fire bans, air quality (AQHI).

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: What does an area restriction order mean for a hunter?
back: No entering or staying inside without written authorization, for any purpose, including hunting.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Evacuation order lifted. Area restriction still on. Hunt?
back: No. Restrictions can outlast evacuation orders.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Ticket for entering a restricted area?
back: Fire centre notices cite $1,150 violation tickets.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Which way does fire spread fastest?
back: Uphill. Rising heat pre heats the fuel above.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Terrain fire traps?
back: Upslopes, chimneys (narrow draws), saddles, heavy dry timber.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Escape direction from a wildfire?
back: Down and across the slope, toward burned ground, rock, water or a road. Never uphill ahead of it.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Cornered by fire, last resort?
back: Bare ground, lie face down low with feet toward the flames, cover mouth and nose until it passes.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Ash and sparks falling on you mean?
back: The fire is probably close, within about 1.6 km.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Report a wildfire?
back: 1 800 663 5555 toll free, or *5555 on a cell.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: How can a hunter start a wildfire by parking?
back: Hot exhaust on dry grass. Park on gravel or dirt.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Hazards when hunting a burn?
back: Danger trees, ash pits with smouldering roots, loose rock, flash floods.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: AQHI bands?
back: 1 to 3 low, 4 to 6 moderate, 7 to 10 high, 10+ very high.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: AQHI 10+: what should a hunter do?
back: Reduce or reschedule strenuous activity like a hard climb. People at higher risk avoid it.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Mask for wildfire smoke if you cannot get to cleaner air?
back: A well fitted N95 respirator.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Heat stroke vs heat exhaustion: key difference?
back: Heat stroke: confused, hot, may stop sweating, 40 °C or more. Call 911.

deck: Wildfire, smoke and heat
front: Heat stroke first aid?
back: Call 911, shade, strip extra clothes, soak with cold water, fan, cold packs on neck, armpits, groin. No aspirin or acetaminophen.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Which slope angles produce most avalanches?
back: 30 to 45 degrees. 25 to 30 less often. Over 45 snow usually sluffs.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: How small a slope can still be dangerous?
back: About 10 m by 10 m can hold enough snow (Avalanche Canada).

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: How much snow on a grass or rock slab slope can slide early season?
back: About 30 cm (Avalanche Canada warning).

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Can an avalanche reach flat ground below?
back: Yes. It can run across flat ground and even uphill.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Name 4 terrain traps.
back: Gullies or creek beds, cliffs below, trees and rocks in the path, flat ground right below a steep slope.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Signs of unstable snow?
back: Recent avalanches (last 48 hours), whumpfs, shooting cracks, hollow sounds, remote triggers.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: No warning signs today. Safe?
back: No. The absence of signs does not mean no danger.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: The 5 danger levels?
back: Low, Moderate, Considerable, High, Extreme.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Which danger level has the most deaths?
back: Considerable (3). Many slopes should be avoided.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Danger rated High: what do you do?
back: Avoid all avalanche terrain. Mellow slopes or dense trees with no overhead hazard.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: The 3 terrain classes (ATES)?
back: Simple, challenging, complex.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: When do Avalanche Canada daily forecasts usually start?
back: Late November in past years (about 22 to 25 November). Before then, read the early season conditions page.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Avalanche rescue gear per person?
back: Transceiver (worn, on), probe and shovel (in the pack on your back). All three, everyone.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: How do you cross a slope that could slide?
back: One at a time, safe spot to safe spot, partner watching.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Caught in an avalanche?
back: Yell, move to the side at 45 degrees, grab a tree, fight to the surface, air space and one hand up as it slows.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Survival of fully buried people over time?
back: Over 90% in the first 15 to 20 minutes, about 35% by 35 minutes. Companion rescue is the best chance.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Companion rescue order?
back: Last seen point, transceiver search, probe, shovel from downhill, face first.

deck: Avalanche awareness for hunters
front: Course to take before alpine hunts in snow?
back: AST 1 (Avalanche Skills Training 1).

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Canadian Red Cross clear ice thickness: alone, group, snowmobile?
back: 15 cm, 20 cm, 25 cm. Floating ice is never 100% safe.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Ice colour and strength?
back: Clear blue strongest, white about half as strong, grey unsafe.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: On white ice, what do you do with the thickness numbers?
back: Double them.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Where is ice thinnest?
back: Inlets, outlets, springs, moving water, edges by reeds and logs, patches ducks kept open.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Why is ice near where ducks sat dangerous?
back: Birds kept that water open longer, so the ice there is very thin.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: How do you test ice?
back: Look from shore for open water, grey or slush; chisel and measure; test again every few steps.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Two hunters crossing ice: side by side?
back: No. Spread out with a gap, PFDs on, picks on your neck.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Ice kit?
back: Ice picks, PFD, floating throw rope, chisel, phone in a dry bag, dry clothes in the truck.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: A duck falls on thin ice. Retrieve it?
back: No. Let it go. Plan shots so birds fall on open water or land.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: In the water: take off your heavy coat?
back: No. Winter clothes trap air for warmth and flotation.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Fell through: which way do you face?
back: Back the way you came. That ice held you.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: How do you get out of an ice hole?
back: Arms on the solid ice, kick flat, dig in picks, slide out on your belly.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Out of the hole: stand up?
back: No. Lie flat and roll away several body lengths.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Someone else falls in: order of help?
back: Call 911, then preach, reach, throw, row. Go only as a last resort.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Run to the edge of the hole to help?
back: No. You may go in too. Reach or throw from solid ground.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: After a cold water rescue, why handle gently?
back: Afterdrop and sudden collapse can follow rescue. Keep them flat, rewarm the trunk.

deck: Ice and cold water: crossing, falling in, self rescue
front: Wading a cold creek?
back: Face upstream, pole as a third leg, hip belt open, one foot at a time. Over the knee and fast: find another way.
